newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba ready to establish links with United States.
newsitem.headline: Cuba ready to establish links with United States.

text.p: HAVANA, May 25 (Reuter) Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina believes Cuba is ready to establish relations with the United States on the basis of respect for the principles of independence, sovereignty and mutual non-interference.
Speaking on Cuban radio on Saturday night, Robaina said: "We are interested in having relations with the United States, at any time, with only one condition: that there are no conditions."
His declarations were carried in Sunday's Juventud Rebelde.

While the Cuban position is not new, some Western diplomats believe its reiteration at this time is a reply to the Clinton administration's demand that Cuba institute major political reforms before the United States will seek an improvement in relations.

Last week, Michael Ranneberger, coordinator for Cuban affairs at the U.S. State Department said: "The message to Cuba is that if there is a process of change, there will be a response (from the United States)."
Western diplomats here said Robaina's statement that no prior conditions would be accepted was a clear rejection of the Clinton administration's policy.

The United States broke diplomatic relations with Cuba on Jan. 1, 1961, two years after Fidel Castro's revolutionary triumph. At that time the administration of President Dwight Eisenhower was already making plans for a CIA-directed invasion of the Caribbean island aimed at overthowing Castro's communist government.
The invasion by Cuban-exiles, trained and financed by the United States government, took place in April 1961 and was defeated by Castro's forces in 72 hours.
In October 1962 the world was brought to the brink of nuclear war when President John F. Kennedy demanded that the Soviet Union remove its missiles with nuclear warheads from Cuba.
Soviet leader Nikita Krushchev said at the time that Kennedy had agreed not to invade Cuba in exchange for the withdrawal of the missiles.
Havana and Washington still do not have full diplomatic relations but each has so-called "Interest Sections" in the others capital to handle consular and other matters.

The closest the two countries came to detente was when President Jimmy Carter agreed to the establishment of the Interest Sections and at the same time lifted the ban on travel by United States' citizens to the socialist island.

Prior to Carter, all U.S passports were stamped: "Not valid for travel to Cuba." At present U.S citizens are prohibited from going to Cuba by the Trading with the Enemy Act which makes any financial dealing with Cuba and expenditures on the island illegal.
The law does not apply to those having a valid professional interest in Cuba, such as journalists, scholars, researchers, priests and pastors.
